screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what atomicity means in Redis and how the MULTI/EXEC pattern and WATCH support reliable multi-command updates. Start by thinking of a bank transfer: money must leave one account and arrive in another, or the system is inconsistent. Redis gives us atomic single commands, but complex updates need grouping. MULTI queues commands on the server and then EXEC runs them all in one uninterrupted sequence. WATCH provides optimistic locking when you must ensure data hasn't changed between reading and writing. We will walk through Python examples that show queuing, execution, and retry behavior when concurrent clients modify keys. You will also see the limitation: Redis transactions do not rollback on internal command failures, so other queued commands still run even if one fails. Finally, we'll compare when to use Lua scripts instead, because a Lua script executes on the server atomically and can encapsulate conditional logic without round trips. By the end, you will understand how to choose between MULTI/EXEC, WATCH, and Lua for consistent Redis updates, and you will be ready to implement safe, retryable workflows in your applications.

screens.title: What atomicity means in Redis
screens.narratorSegment: Atomicity is the guarantee that a sequence of operations behaves as an indivisible unit. In Redis, individual commands like INCR or SADD are atomic by nature: each completes entirely before the server processes the next command, so you don't need locks for single-command updates. But many real-world changes require several commands to happen together — decrementing stock and recording a purchase, or transferring balance between two accounts. For these cases, Redis provides transactions via MULTI and EXEC. MULTI starts queuing commands; EXEC sends the batch to be run sequentially and atomically. That atomicity means that no other client's commands interleave with the queued commands while EXEC runs. A common misconception is to think MULTI/EXEC provides rollback like relational databases: it does not. If one queued command fails when executed, Redis will still apply the other commands and return an error entry in the results array. Practically, that means you must design transactions to avoid commands that can fail due to type or unexpected values, or you must validate inputs before queuing commands. Think of atomicity as either all intended changes become visible together or you detect an abort and retry; but do not assume automatic rollback of partial failures. How will you apply this to an inventory or payment flow to keep operations consistent?

keyIdea.title: Atomicity defined
keyIdea.text: Single commands are atomic; MULTI/EXEC groups commands so they execute as one uninterrupted sequence but without rollback on per-command failures.

content.html:
Definition

Atomicity in Redis

An operation is atomic when it completes entirely or not at all from the perspective of other clients. Redis commands are atomic individually; MULTI/EXEC groups commands to run as a single sequence without interleaving.

Single-command example: INCR counter is atomic.
Multi-command need: decrement stock and push purchaser to purchases list together.
Misconception: MULTI/EXEC does not rollback other commands if one command fails during execution.
Analogy
Bank transfer analogy

A transfer must debit one account and credit another together. If only one side applies, the system is inconsistent. MULTI/EXEC ensures a sequence runs without other operations interleaving, preserving that property when properly designed.

Key Takeaway

Atomicity prevents interleaving but not partial-apply rollback. Validate commands and handle errors at the application level.

screens.title: MULTI and EXEC mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: MULTI and EXEC create a simple, reliable process for queuing and committing a sequence of Redis commands. The process starts with MULTI, which tells the server to begin buffering commands for your client. Every subsequent command is queued rather than executed immediately. When you send EXEC, Redis runs the queued commands sequentially and returns their results as an array in the same order you queued them. This atomic execution means no other client’s commands can run in between the queued operations. A useful mental model is: MULTI marks the start of a local command buffer, queue commands as intended changes, then EXEC flushes and applies them all together. Remember the key limitation: if one of those commands fails at execution time because of a type mismatch or invalid input, Redis does not roll back the prior commands in that EXEC; instead, the failing command’s error is reported in the results array while other commands still apply. That difference is essential when you design transactional sequences. Practice writing small queue-and-commit sequences and inspect the results array to understand which commands succeeded and which returned errors.

keyIdea.title: Queue then commit
keyIdea.text: MULTI begins buffering; commands are queued; EXEC runs them sequentially and returns an ordered results array — errors do not trigger rollback.

content.html:
Process Flow
1. MULTI
Start queuing commands. Subsequent commands are buffered.
2. Queue commands
Call the operations you want executed as a single sequence.
3. EXEC
All queued commands are executed sequentially and atomically from the perspective of other clients.
Inspecting results
EXEC returns an array of replies matching queued commands. Errors appear in the array at the position of the failing command.
No automatic rollback: design transactions to avoid commands that can fail or validate before queueing.
Key Takeaway

Treat MULTI/EXEC as an atomic commit mechanism without rollback. Check results and handle errors in application code.

screens.title: Python pipeline example: inventory update
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical Python example that demonstrates queuing and atomic execution. The example initializes an item's stock and then uses a Redis pipeline to decrement stock and push a purchaser ID onto a purchases list inside a single execute call. The pipeline queues calls such as decr and lpush and then execute sends them as a single atomic batch. When you run the code, the pipeline returns an array of results for each queued command: the new stock value and the length of the list after pushing. This example shows two important behaviors: first, the queue-and-execute pattern ensures those two updates are applied together as one sequence without interleaving from other clients. Second, inspect the returned results array to confirm the new stock and the list state. A misconception to avoid is assuming the pipeline will roll back if one command fails — it will not. If a queued command fails due to a type mismatch, the error appears in the results but other commands still run. When adapting this pattern to production, validate values before queuing and handle errors in the results array to keep your application consistent.

keyIdea.title: Example result
keyIdea.text: Using a pipeline with execute queues commands on the client and runs them atomically on EXEC; check the returned results for success or per-command errors.

content.html:
Starter code (Python)
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

item_id = "product:123"
user_id = "user:abc"

r.set(f"{item_id}:stock", 10)  # Initialize stock

# Start a transaction
pipe = r.pipeline()
pipe.decr(f"{item_id}:stock")
pipe.lpush(f"{item_id}:purchases", user_id)

# Execute all commands atomically
results = pipe.execute()
print(f"Transaction results: {results}")  # [9, 1] - new stock, list length

print(f"Current stock for {item_id}: {r.get(f'{item_id}:stock')}")
print(f"Purchases for {item_id}: {r.lrange(f'{item_id}:purchases', 0, -1)}")
What to watch for
  • Check the results array: each queued command produces a reply or an error entry.
  • Validate types before queueing to avoid runtime errors in EXEC.
  • Use pipelines and MULTI when commands must be applied together for consistency.
Concrete example
Decrement stock and push purchaser ID together so inventory and purchase logs stay in sync after a successful EXEC.
Common mistake
Assuming EXEC will rollback on a failing command. It will not — handle errors explicitly.

screens.title: Optimistic locking with WATCH
screens.narratorSegment: WATCH provides optimistic locking in Redis and is essential when your update depends on the value you read earlier. The pattern is: WATCH keys you care about, read the current values, then start a MULTI and queue the updates you want to make. When you call EXEC, Redis checks whether any of the watched keys changed since you issued WATCH. If any watched key was modified by another client, EXEC will abort and return None (or an empty result in some clients). Your application must detect this result and retry the sequence from the beginning, re-reading values and attempting the WATCH/MULTI/EXEC again. This pattern is effective for check-and-set workflows where you must ensure the value you base your update on is still current at commit time. A common confusion is to leave WATCH blocks open while performing heavy computation or external calls; avoid that. Keep the region between WATCH and EXEC as short and fast as possible to reduce the chance of aborts. Also, when you intentionally give up before executing, call UNWATCH or reset the pipeline so you release the optimistic locks. The essential idea: WATCH lets you detect conflicts at commit time and retry, rather than preventing them with pessimistic locks.

keyIdea.title: WATCH behavior
keyIdea.text: WATCH monitors keys and causes EXEC to abort if those keys change between WATCH and EXEC; applications must detect aborts and retry.

content.html:
Definition

Optimistic locking with WATCH

WATCH monitors one or more keys. If any watched key is modified before EXEC, the transaction aborts and your code should retry.

When to use
When updates depend on previously read values and you want to detect conflicts at commit time.
Retry pattern
If EXEC returns None or WatchError occurs, re-read values and attempt WATCH/MULTI/EXEC again.
Pitfall
Keeping WATCH active across slow or external operations increases abort rates and reduces throughput. Keep the window short.

screens.title: Implementing transfer_funds with WATCH
screens.narratorSegment: This code example implements a safe transfer between two user balances using WATCH to detect concurrent modifications. The function watches both balance keys, reads the current balances, validates the funds, then queues set operations in a MULTI block. If EXEC detects that either watched key changed, it returns None or the client raises a WatchError, and the code retries the entire sequence. The pattern uses a loop with try-except and resets the pipeline in a finally block so the pipeline is clean for the next attempt. A concrete benefit is preventing lost updates: if another process modifies one of the balances while you decide, your EXEC will not silently overwrite that change; instead, you'll retry with the new data. A common misconception is that WATCH prevents other clients from writing — it does not. WATCH only signals the server to abort if a change happens before EXEC. Therefore, handle retries with exponential backoff or short random sleeps to avoid busy-waiting under contention. This example shows robust handling and ensures eventual success or a clear failure if funds are insufficient. Implementing transfer_funds with WATCH means wrap watch/multi/exec in a retry loop and reset the pipeline to handle watcherror or aborted exec results safely.. In practical terms, a python example that retries on watcherror. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Retry logic
keyIdea.text: Wrap WATCH/MULTI/EXEC in a retry loop and reset the pipeline to handle WatchError or aborted EXEC results safely.

content.html:
Safe transfer (Python)
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

user_balance_key = "user:101:balance"
r.set(user_balance_key, 100)  # Initial balance

def transfer_funds(from_user, to_user, amount):
    with r.pipeline() as pipe:
        while True:
            try:
                pipe.watch(from_user, to_user)

                from_balance = int(pipe.get(from_user))
                to_balance = int(pipe.get(to_user))

                if from_balance < amount:
                    pipe.unwatch()
                    return False

                pipe.multi()
                pipe.set(from_user, from_balance - amount)
                pipe.set(to_user, to_balance + amount)

                results = pipe.execute()
                if results is None:
                    continue
                else:
                    return True
            except redis.exceptions.WatchError:
                continue
            finally:
                pipe.reset()
Key behaviors
  • WATCH observes keys; EXEC aborts if they changed.
  • Retry the whole sequence after an abort by looping and re-watching.
  • Call unwatch or reset when you intentionally stop the transaction.
Practical tip
Add short randomized sleep on retry to limit contention under high concurrency.

keyIdea.title: Like feature pattern
keyIdea.text: WATCH the count and set, re-check membership, then MULTI/EXEC to increment count and add the user; retry on abort to maintain correctness.

content.html:
Starter code
import redis
import time
import random
import threading

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

POST_ID = "post:123"
LIKES_COUNT_KEY = f"{POST_ID}:likes_count"
LIKED_BY_KEY = f"{POST_ID}:liked_by"

r.set(LIKES_COUNT_KEY, 0)
r.delete(LIKED_BY_KEY)

def like_post(post_id, user_id):
    with r.pipeline() as pipe:
        while True:
            try:
                pipe.watch(LIKES_COUNT_KEY, LIKED_BY_KEY)

                if pipe.sismember(LIKED_BY_KEY, user_id):
                    pipe.unwatch()
                    return False

                pipe.multi()
                pipe.incr(LIKES_COUNT_KEY)
                pipe.sadd(LIKED_BY_KEY, user_id)

                results = pipe.execute()

                if results is None:
                    time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05))
                    continue
                else:
                    return True

            except redis.exceptions.WatchError:
                time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05))
                continue
            except Exception as e:
                return False
Exercise steps
  1. Initialize keys for a post: count to 0 and an empty set for likers.
  2. Run multiple threads that call like_post with different user IDs.
  3. Observe final count and set membership to confirm correctness.
Watchful note
Watching both the count and the set is safe, but watch only necessary keys to reduce aborts.

screens.title: Limitations of MULTI/EXEC and error handling
screens.narratorSegment: A critical limitation of Redis transactions is the absence of automatic rollback when a command fails during execution. In relational databases, a failing statement typically rolls back the whole transaction. In Redis, MULTI/EXEC guarantees atomic execution with respect to interleaving, but it does not reverse commands that succeeded earlier in the same EXEC if a later command fails. For example, if you try to DECR a key whose value is a non-integer string, that specific command will fail and return an error, while other queued commands will still be executed. The consequence is that partial side effects are possible and must be handled by the application. The right approach is to validate state before queueing potentially failing commands, or handle error results in the returned array explicitly. Another limitation is that WATCH-based retries can lead to livelock under extreme contention if all clients continuously retry. Practical mitigations include reducing the watched key set, keeping the watch window short, adding randomized backoff on retries, and using server-side Lua scripting when the logic is complex and would otherwise require many round trips.

Comparison
Relational DB transaction
Typically supports rollback: if a statement fails, the whole transaction can be undone.
Redis MULTI/EXEC
Executes queued commands atomically relative to other clients, but does not rollback if a command fails during execution.
Type errors still produce side effects in the same EXEC.
WATCH aborts require explicit retry logic.
Lua scripting avoids these multi-round-trip problems by running server-side atomically.
Key Takeaway

Expect to handle partial failures manually: validate earlier, check results, and design retry strategies or use Lua when rollback semantics are required.

screens.title: When to use Lua scripting
screens.narratorSegment: Lua scripting in Redis is the most robust way to perform complex, conditional, or iterative logic atomically on the server. A Lua script runs as a single Redis command: the server executes the whole script without interleaving other clients’ commands. This removes the need to watch keys and retry client-side loops, and it prevents round-trip inefficiencies when you must iterate over collections or perform multiple dependent checks. Use Lua when your operation requires conditional branches, loops, or multiple reads that must happen logically together with writes. However, keep scripts efficient and short to avoid long-running server tasks. A common pattern is to use MULTI/EXEC and WATCH for simple check-and-set flows and to prefer Lua when the logic would otherwise cause multiple retries or many round trips. Remember that Lua scripts replace the need to implement complex retry logic at the client: the full conditional behavior executes atomically on the server and returns a single result indicating success or failure. Architecture decision

When to pick Lua

Use Lua when
  • You need conditional checks and updates that must be atomic.
  • You must iterate or compute over server data without many round trips.
Use WATCH/MULTI when
  • Updates are simple and validations are inexpensive.
  • Retries on conflicts are acceptable and cheap.
Lua is a powerful escalation: it provides full atomicity with conditional logic server-side and avoids complex client retry loops at the cost of moving logic into the Redis server.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of recurring mistakes developers make with Redis transactions. First, misunderstanding rollback: assuming MULTI/EXEC will revert earlier commands if a later one fails. The fix is to validate state before queueing commands and to inspect the results array after EXEC. Second, long-running logic between WATCH and EXEC: if you perform heavy computation or external calls in that window, you increase the chance of aborts and contention. Keep the window short and move heavy work before WATCH if it does not rely on the watched keys. Third, over-watching keys: watch only what matters. Watching many keys increases spurious aborts and reduces throughput. Fourth, failing to unwatch or reset the pipeline when intentionally aborting leads to unexpected behavior; call UNWATCH or pipe. reset() when you need to bail out. Finally, not retrying WATCH transactions: if EXEC returns None or a WatchError occurs, you must implement retry logic to re-read and attempt the transaction again. Apply small randomized backoffs to avoid livelock under contention. These patterns will help your system behave reliably under concurrency. screens.title: Assessment: inventory DECR type error scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Consider the assessment scenario: you use MULTI/EXEC to decrement stock and add an order ID, but the stock key holds a string that cannot be interpreted as an integer. What happens when DECR runs inside EXEC? The correct understanding is that Redis executes queued commands sequentially under EXEC, but it does not roll back other commands if one fails. So the DECR command will fail and return an error in the corresponding slot of the results array. However, other commands queued in the same EXEC, like adding the order ID to a list, will still be executed. The transaction completes in the sense that all queued commands were attempted; some may have errored. The practical outcome is partial application and an inconsistent state unless application logic validates or prevents such type mismatches before queueing commands. screens.title: Practical checklist before using MULTI/EXEC
screens.narratorSegment: Before wrapping code in MULTI/EXEC or WATCH, run through a short checklist to keep transactions predictable. First, validate inputs and data types to avoid command failures inside EXEC. Second, identify the minimal set of keys that must be watched; smaller watch sets reduce abort rates. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what atomicity means in Redis and how the MULTI/EXEC pattern and WATCH support reliable multi-command updates. Start by thinking of a bank transfer: money must leave one account and arrive in another, or the system is inconsistent. Redis gives us atomic single commands, but complex updates need grouping. MULTI queues commands on the server and then EXEC runs them all in one uninterrupted sequence. WATCH provides optimistic locking when you must ensure data hasn't changed between reading and writing. We will walk through Python examples that show queuing, execution, and retry behavior when concurrent clients modify keys. You will also see the limitation: Redis transactions do not rollback on internal command failures, so other queued commands still run even if one fails. Finally, we'll compare when to use Lua scripts instead, because a Lua script executes on the server atomically and can encapsulate conditional logic without round trips. By the end, you will understand how to choose between MULTI/EXEC, WATCH, and Lua for consistent Redis updates, and you will be ready to implement safe, retryable workflows in your applications.

These objectives describe concrete skills you will build as you work through the chapter. First, you will be able to explain atomicity in Redis: what it means for an operation to be indivisible and why that matters for data integrity. Second, you will learn how to use MULTI and EXEC to batch commands so a set of updates happens as a single sequence. Third, you'll practice implementing optimistic locking with WATCH to ensure conditional updates only commit if keys have not changed. And fourth, you will learn to identify common pitfalls such as type errors inside transactions and long-running WATCH blocks. Each objective ties directly to a hands-on coding pattern so you can not only describe the behaviors but also implement and test them in Python. As you study, think about simple concrete scenarios — a bank transfer, an order purchase, or a like button — and imagine how these skills keep those operations correct under concurrency.

In the next part of the objectives we focus on applying transactional patterns and learning safe behaviors. You will practice writing retry loops that detect transaction aborts and re-run the WATCH/MULTI/EXEC sequence, and you will practice releasing watches when you abort an operation to avoid holding optimistic locks unnecessarily. You will also learn to choose the narrowest set of keys to WATCH, because watching too many keys increases the chance of spurious aborts. Finally, you will learn when to escalate: if your logic requires conditional branching, loops over collections, or tight server-side checks that would become many round trips, you will prefer a Lua script executed on the server because it runs atomically and avoids race windows. Each of these application skills is essential: safe retry patterns keep systems correct under concurrency, releasing watches prevents dead windows of contention, and knowing when to use Lua prevents inefficient client-server loops.

Atomicity is the guarantee that a sequence of operations behaves as an indivisible unit. In Redis, individual commands like INCR or SADD are atomic by nature: each completes entirely before the server processes the next command, so you don't need locks for single-command updates. But many real-world changes require several commands to happen together — decrementing stock and recording a purchase, or transferring balance between two accounts. For these cases, Redis provides transactions via MULTI and EXEC. MULTI starts queuing commands; EXEC sends the batch to be run sequentially and atomically. That atomicity means that no other client's commands interleave with the queued commands while EXEC runs. A common misconception is to think MULTI/EXEC provides rollback like relational databases: it does not. If one queued command fails when executed, Redis will still apply the other commands and return an error entry in the results array. Practically, that means you must design transactions to avoid commands that can fail due to type or unexpected values, or you must validate inputs before queuing commands. Think of atomicity as either all intended changes become visible together or you detect an abort and retry; but do not assume automatic rollback of partial failures. How will you apply this to an inventory or payment flow to keep operations consistent?

MULTI and EXEC create a simple, reliable process for queuing and committing a sequence of Redis commands. The process starts with MULTI, which tells the server to begin buffering commands for your client. Every subsequent command is queued rather than executed immediately. When you send EXEC, Redis runs the queued commands sequentially and returns their results as an array in the same order you queued them. This atomic execution means no other client’s commands can run in between the queued operations. A useful mental model is: MULTI marks the start of a local command buffer, queue commands as intended changes, then EXEC flushes and applies them all together. Remember the key limitation: if one of those commands fails at execution time because of a type mismatch or invalid input, Redis does not roll back the prior commands in that EXEC; instead, the failing command’s error is reported in the results array while other commands still apply. That difference is essential when you design transactional sequences. Practice writing small queue-and-commit sequences and inspect the results array to understand which commands succeeded and which returned errors.

Let's walk through a practical Python example that demonstrates queuing and atomic execution. The example initializes an item's stock and then uses a Redis pipeline to decrement stock and push a purchaser ID onto a purchases list inside a single execute call. The pipeline queues calls such as decr and lpush and then execute sends them as a single atomic batch. When you run the code, the pipeline returns an array of results for each queued command: the new stock value and the length of the list after pushing. This example shows two important behaviors: first, the queue-and-execute pattern ensures those two updates are applied together as one sequence without interleaving from other clients. Second, inspect the returned results array to confirm the new stock and the list state. A misconception to avoid is assuming the pipeline will roll back if one command fails — it will not. If a queued command fails due to a type mismatch, the error appears in the results but other commands still run. When adapting this pattern to production, validate values before queuing and handle errors in the results array to keep your application consistent.

WATCH provides optimistic locking in Redis and is essential when your update depends on the value you read earlier. The pattern is: WATCH keys you care about, read the current values, then start a MULTI and queue the updates you want to make. When you call EXEC, Redis checks whether any of the watched keys changed since you issued WATCH. If any watched key was modified by another client, EXEC will abort and return None (or an empty result in some clients). Your application must detect this result and retry the sequence from the beginning, re-reading values and attempting the WATCH/MULTI/EXEC again. This pattern is effective for check-and-set workflows where you must ensure the value you base your update on is still current at commit time. A common confusion is to leave WATCH blocks open while performing heavy computation or external calls; avoid that. Keep the region between WATCH and EXEC as short and fast as possible to reduce the chance of aborts. Also, when you intentionally give up before executing, call UNWATCH or reset the pipeline so you release the optimistic locks. The essential idea: WATCH lets you detect conflicts at commit time and retry, rather than preventing them with pessimistic locks.

This code example implements a safe transfer between two user balances using WATCH to detect concurrent modifications. The function watches both balance keys, reads the current balances, validates the funds, then queues set operations in a MULTI block. If EXEC detects that either watched key changed, it returns None or the client raises a WatchError, and the code retries the entire sequence. The pattern uses a loop with try-except and resets the pipeline in a finally block so the pipeline is clean for the next attempt. A concrete benefit is preventing lost updates: if another process modifies one of the balances while you decide, your EXEC will not silently overwrite that change; instead, you'll retry with the new data. A common misconception is that WATCH prevents other clients from writing — it does not. WATCH only signals the server to abort if a change happens before EXEC. Therefore, handle retries with exponential backoff or short random sleeps to avoid busy-waiting under contention. This example shows robust handling and ensures eventual success or a clear failure if funds are insufficient. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The pattern requires WATCH to prevent race conditions where two concurrent likes could cause inconsistent state. The recommended flow is: WATCH the likes_count and liked_by keys, check whether the user already liked the post (optional optimization), then start MULTI to increment the counter and add the user to the set. If another client modified those keys concurrently, EXEC will abort and you must retry. A critical limitation of Redis transactions is the absence of automatic rollback when a command fails during execution. In relational databases, a failing statement typically rolls back the whole transaction. In Redis, MULTI/EXEC guarantees atomic execution with respect to interleaving, but it does not reverse commands that succeeded earlier in the same EXEC if a later command fails. For example, if you try to DECR a key whose value is a non-integer string, that specific command will fail and return an error, while other queued commands will still be executed. The consequence is that partial side effects are possible and must be handled by the application. The right approach is to validate state before queueing potentially failing commands, or handle error results in the returned array explicitly. Another limitation is that WATCH-based retries can lead to livelock under extreme contention if all clients continuously retry. Practical mitigations include reducing the watched key set, keeping the watch window short, adding randomized backoff on retries, and using server-side Lua scripting when the logic is complex and would otherwise require many round trips.

Lua scripting in Redis is the most robust way to perform complex, conditional, or iterative logic atomically on the server. A Lua script runs as a single Redis command: the server executes the whole script without interleaving other clients’ commands. This removes the need to watch keys and retry client-side loops, and it prevents round-trip inefficiencies when you must iterate over collections or perform multiple dependent checks. Use Lua when your operation requires conditional branches, loops, or multiple reads that must happen logically together with writes. However, keep scripts efficient and short to avoid long-running server tasks.
